newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ yields sell into close in absence of new govt.
newsitem.headline: NZ yields sell into close in absence of new govt.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD
OVERNIGHT CASH 9.05 PCT (PREV 9.05) US 5-YR 5.96 (PREV 5.97)
* NZ yields sell into close in absence of new coalition govt
* NZ First talks drag on
* Short term market movements impossible to predict
New Zealand bond yields crept higher at Tuesday's close as the market began to lose its nerve in the face of protracted discussions over the shape of the country's new government.
Political power-broker New Zealand First began a caucus of MPs at 10.30 a.m. (2130 GMT) to choose a coalition partner between the conservative National Party and the centre-left Labour Party.
The meeting was still going at 5.10 p.m., with no sign of an announcement scheduled for 5.00 p.m. (0400 GMT) or soon after about when and how NZ First expected to release its final decision.
The last half hour of trade saw a fairly sharp sell-off in the bonds, with the 02/00s ending nine basis points higher in yield at 7.06 percent and the 10-years off 10 at 7.28 percent.
In the money market, 90-day rates climbed a couple of basis points and the December futures contract was off six at 91.57.
If NZ First swings Labour's way it would spell the end of six years of conservative government, and an increase in social spending which has financial markets concerned.

New Zealand has been without a formal government since a general election on October 12, the country's first under a proportional representation system which left NZ First, with only 13 percent of the party vote, in a position to decide which of the two main parties it would return to power.
One bond dealer said there was very little information yet for the market to trade on.
"It's always been a toss of the coin. Appreciating one thing the negotiators have done well is they've said nothing particular...so opinions are just that," he said.
"Most people would have you believe yields will go up if it's Labour, down if it's National, but that's relatively simplistic stuff.

"You're not going to get that much detail straight away. It's all fine and dandy for them to say Labour or National, but if they don't front up and play some sort of open misere hand, and say here's what we agreed to and here's how we're going to govern, there is not a great deal you can draw from it."
